raw_case_text: The 57-year-old was an African male, originally from Rwanda, from where he initially immigrated to Russia. He lived in Russia for 20 years (1984-2004) before he eventually immigrated to Canada in 2004. He started to experience right shoulder pain and stiffness in 2010. There was no history of trauma to the joint and morning stiffness nor involvement of other joints. The right shoulder pain and stiffness progressed in severity over the ensuing three years and became debilitating, limiting his ability to work in construction. He had undergone multiple courses of physiotherapy and had been prescribed high doses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications without a meaningful response. For the six months prior to presentation, he had been experiencing night sweats without accompanying fever, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. He did give a history of exposure to MTb while living in Russia as one of his workmates developed pulmonary Tb; however, our patient was not investigated at that time. Examination of the right shoulder revealed minimal swelling and that erythema and warmth were absent, but there was a decreased range of motion. Due to the worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness, a plain radiograph of the chest and shoulder was performed, revealing only an old clavicular injury and that the acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints were intact. Neither acute nor chronic parenchymal lung, bone, or joint space abnormalities were observed. An X-ray (Figure 1) and MRI (Figure 2) of the right shoulder were therefore performed, demonstrating intra-articular effusion and erosions of articular margins, compatible with a septic joint. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 68, and HIV test result was negative. Operative drainage and debridement were undertaken, and the thick purulent joint fluid subsequently yielded MTb by direct smear examination with Ziehl-Neelsen staining and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), the Xpert MTB/RIF test, establishing the diagnosis of osteoarticular Tb. Antituberculosis therapy was therefore initiated with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) in addition to pyridoxine. The subsequent Tb culture revealed no resistance to the standard first-line regimen RIPE. He was treated with RIPE for 2 months followed by rifampin and isoniazid for 10 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male presented with debilitating right shoulder pain and stiffness progressing over 3 years and night sweats for 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 57-year-old male noticed insidious right shoulder pain and stiffness that progressively worsened over 3 years, eventually limiting his ability to work in construction. He had completed multiple courses of physiotherapy and high-dose NSAIDs without symptomatic benefit. Over the 6 months prior to evaluation, he experienced recurrent night sweats without fever, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. He had an occupational exposure to a coworker with active pulmonary tuberculosis while living in Russia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immigrated from Rwanda to Russia (resided 1984-2004), then to Canada in 2004. Known occupational exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis in Russia (uninvestigated). Old clavicular trauma. Multiple courses of physiotherapy and high-dose NSAIDs without relief.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right shoulder pain, severe stiffness, and night sweats for 6 months. Negative for fever, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, morning stiffness, or symptoms in other joints. Home medications: high-dose NSAIDs. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right shoulder: minimal swelling, decreased active and passive range of motion; erythema and warmth absent. Clavicular deformity consistent with remote fracture. Remainder of physical examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: ESR 68 mm/h. HIV serology negative. Initial plain radiographs of chest and shoulder: remote clavicular fracture; acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints intact without acute parenchymal lung, bone, or joint abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat dedicated right shoulder radiograph and MRI: glenohumeral intra-articular effusion with erosions of articular margins compatible with a septic joint. Operative arthrotomy with drainage and debridement performed, yielding thick purulent joint fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Monoarticular tuberculous arthritis of the right glenohumeral joint (osteoarticular tuberculosis), confirmed by operative drainage yielding purulent joint fluid positive on Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli, positive nucleic acid amplification testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF), and culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis with documented pan-susceptibility to first-line agents. Management & Outcome: Treated with operative drainage and debridement, followed by antituberculosis therapy with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE), and pyridoxine for 2 months, followed by rifampin and isoniazid for 10 months (total duration 12 months). Demonstrated excellent clinical recovery with restoration of shoulder function.
